unit: Ch 3: Financial Analysis and Planning: Ratio Analysis
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Definition, Objectives and Sources of Ratio Analysis
explain: A ratio is a mathematical expression showing the relationship between two connected accounting figures.
Ratio analysis helps evaluate past performance, current financial health, and future growth potential.
Comparisons can be intra-firm (comparing with past years) or inter-firm (comparing with industry peers).
Primary data sources include annual reports, interim statements, notes to accounts, cash flow statements, and business periodicals.

flow.title: Steps in Ratio Analysis Calculation
steps: Select relevant financial statement figures
Establish logical mathematical relationship
Calculate the accounting ratio
Compare with historical or industry benchmarks
Draw conclusions for stakeholder decision making

topics.example: Comparing your current year's sales with last year's sales to see if the business is growing.
remember: Single accounting numbers carry little meaning until related to another benchmark figure.
mistakes: Comparing figures that have no logical connection, such as dividing rent expense by inventory turnover.

quiz.q: Which type of comparison evaluates a firm's ratios against other companies in the same industry?
quiz.why: Inter-firm comparison compares financial performance across different companies within the same industry.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard source of financial data for ratio analysis?
quiz.why: Personal tax returns of directors are private personal records and not corporate financial data sources.

topics.title: Liquidity and Short-Term Solvency Ratios
explain: Liquidity ratios test a business's ability to pay off short-term liabilities as they fall due.
Current Ratio equals Current Assets divided by Current Liabilities, with an ideal benchmark of 2:1.
Quick Ratio (Acid-Test) excludes inventories and prepaid expenses from current assets, with an ideal benchmark of 1:1.
Cash Ratio measures absolute liquidity using cash, bank balances, and marketable securities.
Basic Defense Interval calculates how many days operational expenses can be met using quick cash assets.

flow.title: Assessing Short-Term Solvency
steps: Identify total current assets and liabilities
Calculate Current Ratio against 2:1 standard
Deduct inventory and prepaids for Quick Ratio
Measure Cash Ratio for immediate liquidity
Check Basic Defense Interval for cash runway

topics.example: If a shop has ₹200 cash and quick assets and owes ₹100 due tomorrow, its Quick Ratio is 2:1, showing high liquidity.
remember: Ideal Current Ratio is 2:1; Ideal Quick Ratio is 1:1.
mistakes: Including inventory or prepaid expenses when calculating Quick Assets.

quiz.q: What is the standard ideal benchmark for the Current Ratio?
quiz.why: The generally accepted satisfactory standard benchmark for Current Ratio is 2:1.

quiz.q: Which asset is deducted from Current Assets to compute Quick Assets?
quiz.why: Inventories are deducted because they cannot be immediately converted into cash at short notice without loss.

topics.title: Capital Structure and Long-Term Solvency Ratios
explain: Capital structure ratios evaluate the long-term stability and funding mix of the business.
Equity Ratio measures shareholder funds relative to net assets; a higher ratio implies lower lender risk.
Debt Ratio measures total outside debt relative to net assets or total assets.
Debt to Equity Ratio indicates financial leverage by comparing total debt or long-term debt to shareholders' equity.
Capital Gearing Ratio compares fixed interest/dividend-bearing capital against equity shareholders' funds.
Proprietary Ratio indicates the proportion of total assets financed by shareholders.

flow.title: Capital Structure Risk Assessment
steps: Sum up equity and long-term debt sources
Compute Debt to Equity Ratio
Check Capital Gearing for fixed cost burdens
Assess Proprietary Ratio for asset security
Determine overall long-term financial solvency

topics.example: A firm funded 70% by debt and 30% by equity is highly geared, meaning lenders bear high financial risk.
remember: Capital Gearing Ratio = (Preference Share Capital + Debentures + Borrowings) / (Equity Capital + Reserves - Losses).
mistakes: Including fictitious assets or accumulated losses in Net Worth or Total Assets.

quiz.q: A high Debt to Equity ratio generally indicates:
o: Higher financial leverage and financial risk
quiz.why: Higher debt relative to equity increases financial leverage and fixed interest obligations, raising risk.

quiz.q: In the Capital Gearing Ratio, which item goes into the numerator?
o: Fixed interest and fixed dividend bearing capital
quiz.why: The numerator consists of fixed-return capital like preference shares, debentures, and borrowed funds.

topics.title: Coverage Ratios
explain: Coverage ratios measure the firm's capacity to service its fixed debt and dividend commitments.
Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) measures cash earnings available to pay annual interest and principal installments (ideal ratio is 1.5 to 2).
Interest Coverage Ratio (Times Interest Earned) equals EBIT divided by Interest expense (ideal ratio > 1).
Preference Dividend Coverage Ratio evaluates Profit After Tax (PAT) relative to preference dividend obligations.
Fixed Charges Coverage Ratio tests cash flow before interest and tax against total fixed financing charges.

flow.title: Evaluating Debt Servicing Capacity
steps: Determine EBIT and add back non-cash charges
Calculate Earnings Available for Debt Service
Divide by annual interest plus principal repayments
Compare DSCR against target benchmark of 1.5-2.0
Confirm if loan servicing obligations are safe

topics.example: If a company earns ₹200 EBIT and pays ₹50 annual interest, its Interest Coverage Ratio is 4 times.
remember: EBIT is used in Interest Coverage Ratio because interest is a tax-deductible expense.
mistakes: Using PAT instead of EBIT when calculating Interest Coverage Ratio.

quiz.q: What is the numerator used to compute the Interest Coverage Ratio?
quiz.why: EBIT is used because interest expense is paid out of pre-tax operational earnings.

quiz.q: What is the generally satisfactory benchmark range for Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR)?
quiz.why: A DSCR between 1.5 and 2.0 is considered comfortable by commercial lenders.

topics.title: Activity and Asset Management Ratios
explain: Activity ratios evaluate how efficiently a firm utilizes its assets to generate sales revenue.
Inventory Turnover Ratio equals Cost of Goods Sold (or Sales) divided by Average Inventory.
Receivables Turnover Ratio equals Credit Sales divided by Average Accounts Receivable.
Average Collection Period (in days) equals 365 (or 360) divided by Receivables Turnover Ratio.
Payables Turnover Ratio equals Annual Net Credit Purchases divided by Average Accounts Payable.
Working Capital Turnover Ratio measures how effectively working capital generates sales.

flow.title: Working Capital Cycle Analysis
steps: Compute Inventory Turnover and Holding Period
Calculate Receivables Turnover and Collection Period
Determine Payables Turnover and Payment Period
Combine components to evaluate working capital efficiency

topics.example: If credit sales are ₹12,00,000 and average receivables are ₹2,00,000, receivables turnover is 6 times per year.
remember: Average Collection Period (Days) = 365 / Receivables Turnover Ratio.
mistakes: Using total sales instead of credit sales for Receivables Turnover when credit sales data is provided.

quiz.q: How is the Receivables Collection Period calculated?
quiz.why: Collection period in days is obtained by dividing total days in a year (365) by the turnover ratio.

quiz.q: A low Inventory Turnover Ratio generally indicates:
o: Fast moving stock and high sales efficiency
quiz.why: A low stock turnover ratio implies inventory stays unsold in warehouses for long periods.

topics.title: Profitability Ratios Based on Sales and Overall Return
explain: Profitability ratios measure the operational efficiency and earning capacity of a firm.
Gross Profit Ratio equals (Gross Profit / Sales) × 100.
Net Profit Ratio equals (Net Profit or EAT / Sales) × 100.
Operating Profit Ratio equals (Operating Profit or EBIT / Sales) × 100.
Return on Investment (ROI) evaluates earnings relative to total capital or investment.
Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) equals EBIT(1-t) or EBIT divided by Capital Employed.

flow.title: Analyzing Profitability from Sales to ROI
steps: Determine Gross Profit Margin from trading activities
Deduct operating expenses to find Operating Profit
Deduct tax and interest to compute Net Profit Margin
Calculate ROCE to measure total capital efficiency
Compare overall ROI with borrowing interest rate

topics.example: If sales are ₹1,00,000 and gross profit is ₹25,000, the Gross Profit Ratio is 25%.
remember: ROCE should always exceed the company's borrowing interest rate for favorable gearing.
mistakes: Including fictitious assets like deferred expenses when calculating Capital Employed.

o: Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold minus Operating Expenses
Sales minus Total Expenses including Tax
quiz.why: Operating profit isolates core operational earnings before interest and non-operating items.

quiz.q: Capital Employed can be defined as:
quiz.why: Capital Employed equals Fixed Assets plus Net Working Capital (or Total Assets minus Current Liabilities).

topics.title: Du Pont Analysis for Return on Equity (ROE)
explain: The Du Pont Model breaks down Return on Equity into three distinct components.
Formula: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier.
Net Profit Margin (Profit / Sales) measures profit efficiency per rupee of turnover.
Asset Turnover (Sales / Total Assets) measures asset utilization efficiency.
Equity Multiplier (Total Assets / Shareholders' Equity) measures financial leverage.
It reveals whether ROE is driven by profitability, operational speed, or high debt load.

flow.title: Du Pont ROE Breakdown
steps: Calculate Net Profit Margin (Profit / Sales)
Calculate Asset Turnover (Sales / Assets)
Calculate Equity Multiplier (Assets / Equity)
Multiply all three components together
Analyze key drivers of Return on Equity

topics.example: If Profit Margin is 10%, Asset Turnover is 2, and Equity Multiplier is 1.5, ROE = 0.10 × 2 × 1.5 = 30%.
remember: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier.
mistakes: Confusing Equity Multiplier with Debt-to-Equity Ratio.

quiz.q: In the 3-factor Du Pont Model, Equity Multiplier is calculated as:
quiz.why: Equity Multiplier measures total assets relative to equity capital to reflect financial leverage.

quiz.q: If a company increases debt while keeping assets and profit constant, its ROE under Du Pont model will:
o: Increase due to higher Equity Multiplier
quiz.why: Higher debt reduces equity relative to assets, raising the Equity Multiplier and boosting ROE.

topics.title: Owner's and Market-Based Ratios
explain: Earnings Per Share (EPS) equals Net Profit available to equity shareholders divided by Number of equity shares.
Dividend Per Share (DPS) equals total equity dividend divided by number of equity shares.
Dividend Payout Ratio (DP) equals DPS divided by EPS.
Price-Earnings (P/E) Ratio equals Market Price Per Share (MPS) divided by EPS.
Dividend Yield equals (DPS / MPS) × 100.
Q Ratio (Tobin's Q) compares market value of equity and liabilities to estimated replacement cost of assets.

flow.title: Evaluating Investor Valuation Metrics
steps: Compute Net Profit for Equity Shareholders
Divide by share count to find EPS
Calculate DPS and Dividend Payout Ratio
Divide Market Price per Share by EPS for P/E Ratio
Assess stock valuation relative to market norms

topics.example: If market price per share is ₹100 and EPS is ₹10, the P/E ratio is 10 times.
remember: Tobin's Q Ratio > 1 indicates market overvaluation, while Q < 1 indicates undervaluation.
mistakes: Using total PAT instead of earnings available to equity (after deducting preference dividends) to calculate EPS.

quiz.q: How is the Price-Earnings (P/E) Ratio calculated?
quiz.why: P/E ratio compares market price of share to earnings per share.

quiz.q: A Tobin's Q ratio greater than 1 suggests that the stock is:
quiz.why: When market valuation exceeds replacement cost of assets (Q > 1), the market values the entity higher than asset replacement value.

topics.title: Users, Applications, and Limitations of Ratio Analysis
explain: Different users analyze different ratios: lenders focus on coverage/solvency, creditors look at liquidity, and shareholders focus on profitability/valuation.
Ratios aid performance evaluation, inter-firm comparisons, financial forecasting, and budgeting.
Horizontal Analysis compares statements across multiple years; Vertical Analysis evaluates items within a single year as percentages of a base.
Key limitations include distortion by inflation, seasonal variations, window dressing, differing accounting policies, and lack of absolute standard norms.

flow.title: Conducting Financial Statement Analysis
steps: Gather multi-year financial statements
Apply Horizontal or Vertical analysis techniques
Compute functional ratio sets for stakeholders
Adjust for inflation, seasonality, and window dressing
Provide qualitative insights alongside ratio findings

topics.example: Comparing a company's financial figures for 2021, 2022, and 2023 side-by-side is horizontal analysis.
remember: Ratios provide clues, not definitive conclusions; expert interpretation is required.
mistakes: Assuming a high Current Ratio is always good without checking for idle cash or slow inventory.

quiz.q: Analysing financial statements of a single year by expressing each line item as a percentage of total sales or assets is called:
quiz.why: Vertical analysis evaluates items within a single financial period as percentages of a base figure.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a recognized limitation of Ratio Analysis?
o: Results can be distorted by window dressing and inflation
It cannot be used by shareholders
quiz.why: Window dressing and historical cost distortion due to inflation are major limitations of financial ratios.
